What Cyclospora is and how it spreads
Latest Cyclospora outbreak updates

records.text:
Cyclospora parasite infections are rising across the United States, and many people don't know the warning signs until they become seriously sick. This dangerous foodborne parasite is linked to fresh salads, berries, herbs, and leafy greens. If you or a loved one has diarrhea that lasts for days or keeps coming back, this video could help you understand what is happening.

Dr. William Parker, with 21 years of experience caring for older adults, explains everything you need to know about the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak. Learn how this parasite spreads, why adults over 60 face higher risks, the symptoms to watch for, the correct medical tests to request, proven treatment options, and simple ways to lower your risk this summer.

📌 In This Video You'll Learn:

✅ What Cyclospora is and how people become infected
✅ Why the current Cyclospora outbreak is growing across the U.S.
✅ Common symptoms including watery diarrhea, fatigue, bloating, nausea, and dehydration
✅ Why older adults have a higher risk of serious complications
✅ Foods most commonly linked to Cyclospora infections
✅ How this parasite is different from normal food poisoning
✅ Why many routine stool tests fail to detect Cyclospora
✅ The specific test you can ask your doctor about
✅ The proven antibiotic treatment doctors recommend
✅ Why parasite cleanses and natural remedies are not proven to work
✅ Easy food safety tips to protect yourself and your family

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Cyclospora?
Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, a foodborne illness that mainly spreads through contaminated fresh produce.

What are the symptoms?
Watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, bloating, nausea, loss of appetite, weight loss, fatigue, and dehydration.

How long do symptoms last?
Without proper treatment, symptoms can last for weeks and may improve before returning again.

How is Cyclospora treated?
Doctors usually prescribe the antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole after confirming the diagnosis.

Can washing vegetables remove Cyclospora?
Washing helps reduce dirt but may not completely remove the parasite. Proper food handling and cooking certain foods can lower the risk.

⚠️ Medical Disclaimer

This video is for educational purposes only and should not replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with your healthcare provider if you experience ongoing diarrhea, dehydration, or other concerning symptoms.

FDA foodborne outbreak investigations: https://www.fda.gov/food/outbreaks-fo...
Recalls & food safety: https://www.foodsafety.gov

Why dry mouth is not a normal part of healthy aging
The most common causes of xerostomia
How medications can reduce saliva production
The link between dry mouth, gum disease, and heart health

Easy ways to improve saliva production naturally
Questions to ask your doctor about persistent dry mouth

functional difference at 30 days in
energy, in muscle steadiness, in how
mornings feel will give you real
personal data rather than just a theory.
There is a real difference between
health care that catalogs what's wrong
with you, and health care that builds
the reserve that determines how you
handle what comes next. After 70, that
difference becomes the whole game. The
best physicians I've known in 21 years
of practice are the ones who look at a
patient and ask not just what needs to
be managed, but what needs to be built.
And the answer to that question almost
always traces back to some version of
the six signs we've gone through today.
Something else worth naming directly
because it comes up often in
conversations I have with people over
60, it's easy to look at a list like
this and feel discouraged if you don't
currently have all six in place. That's
the wrong read. Harold, whose story I
opened with, wasn't born with a lean
medication list and a high HDL. Those
things were the output of decades of
mostly unremarkable daily choices that
added up over time. He wasn't perfect at
any of them. He just didn't stop. The
research on longevity consistently shows
that what matters most isn't the quality
of your best days, it's the floor your
worst days don't fall below. And that
floor is built by the kind of ordinary
undramatic consistency that doesn't make
headlines, but shows up clearly in a lab
report and a conversation with a doctor
who's paying attention. You've probably
been told at some point that the goal
after 70 is maintenance. That's not what
the research shows, and it's not what
I've seen in 21 years. You're not just
maintaining, you're either building
reserve or losing it every single day
through the choices that on any given
morning seem too small to matter. You
have every right to understand what your
labs and your habits are actually saying
about your trajectory
and every right to have the conversation
with your doctor that moves from problem
management toward genuine optimization.
Start today with one glass of
protein-rich breakfast and a 20-minute
walk. That's genuinely all it takes to
begin. If this gave you something
useful, go ahead and subscribe, and I'll
see you in the next one.

aggressive spinal fusion surgery for

surgeon reviewing her MRI identified
degenerative disc disease and spinal

movement at the painful segment. Most
people with chronic back pain assume

some patients with specific diagnoses

degenerative changes, the kind of wear
and tear that is common in adults over

greater risk. The complication rate for

distinction between decompression, which

fusion, which eliminates movement at a
spinal segment, is important. Not every
stenosis diagnosis requires fusion,

decompression should be based on
specific instability findings, not
simply on the presence of degeneration.
The practical guidance during to spinal
fusion, ask specifically whether you
have undergone a full trial of
structured physical therapy, not generic

progressive rehabilitation program under

recommendation includes what it
includes. The common mistake is equating

reliably predict either the source of
pain or the response to surgery. The

full discussion. Quick pause. Has a
physician ever talked to you about the
difference between what shows on imaging

comments. This is one of the most
important distinctions in
musculoskeletal medicine and one of the

major cancer removal surgery,
particularly pancreatic cancer. This
surgery category deserves careful

age and overall health.

operate. The geriatric risk assessment

focus now.
What comes next is where the principle

Malnutrition is common and often
identified in older adults facing
surgery, and it directly impairs wound
healing and immune function
postoperatively. A formal preoperative
assessment by a geriatrician or a
comprehensive preoperative medicine
clinic, where available,
significantly improves the precision of
surgical risk assessment and often
identifies correctable factors that
improve outcomes. The common mistake is
treating the word elective as meaning
low risk. Elective means scheduled. It
means there is time to prepare. That
time is valuable. Using it to optimize
your medical status before surgery is
one of the most evidence-based things
you can do to improve your outcome. Now,
here it is, the surgery that changes the
conversation entirely and the one where
everything I've built today comes to
bear most urgently. Because unlike the
previous four, this one often does not
allow time for deliberation. Surgery
five, emergency abdominal surgery in
adults over 75. Emergency abdominal
surgery encompasses a range of
operations performed under urgent or
emergent conditions. Ruptured abdominal
aortic aneurysm, perforated bowels from
diverticulitis or a perforated ulcer,
bowel obstruction requiring surgical
intervention, acute appendicitis, or
other acute abdominal events requiring
immediate operative management. Here is
what makes this surgery category the
most critical on today's list. By
definition, it happens under conditions
that eliminate most of the preparation,
optimization, and deliberation that
improve outcomes in elective surgery.
The patient is acutely ill. The decision
must be made quickly. The family is
often distressed and making decisions
under time pressure without adequate
information about realistic outcomes.
And the baseline medical conditions that
would have been carefully managed before
elective surgery are now being managed
simultaneously with the acute surgical
emergency. The outcomes data for
emergency abdominal surgery in adults
over 75 is sobering and deserves to be
clearly stated. Research published in
the British Journal of Surgery and
multiple other sources has documented
30-day mortality rates following
emergency abdominal surgery in patients
over 75 ranging from 15 to 35% depending
on the specific procedure and the
patient's preoperative status with rates
considerably higher in the frailest
patients. One-year mortality rates in
some studies exceed 50% in patients over
80, and among survivors, functional
decline, loss of independence, reduced
mobility, cognitive deterioration is
common. This is not a reason to refuse
emergency surgery that is genuinely
necessary to preserve life. If a bowel
is perforated and sepsis is developing,
the alternative to surgery is not
comfort, it is death. Emergency surgery
in this context is life-saving, and the
decision to operate is appropriate. What
the data argues is that the outcomes of
emergency abdominal surgery are heavily
influenced by factors that can be
influenced before the emergency occurs.
Nutritional status, frailty level,
advance care planning, and critically,
whether the patient has at some prior
point had an explicit conversation with
their physician and their family about
their wishes in the event of a surgical
emergency, including what level of
intervention is consistent with their
values and goals. The most powerful
intervention for emergency abdominal
surgery outcomes is not something that
happens in the operating room. It is
what happens before the emergency.
Maintaining muscle mass and functional
fitness, which directly determines
physiological reserve. Keeping chronic
conditions well managed, which
determines the baseline the body is
starting from when the acute event
occurs. And having documented advance
directives and goals of care
conversations, which ensures that in a
moment of medical crisis, the decisions
made reflect what the patient would
actually want, rather than defaulting to
maximum intervention in the absence of
guidance. A study published in JAMA
Surgery found that older adults who had
engaged in pre-operative frailty
optimization programs, structured
exercise and nutritional support before
major surgery,
significantly lower complication rates
and faster return to function than
matched controls who had not undergone
prehabilitation. The principle applies
equally to non-elective surgery because
every day of maintained fitness before
an emergency is a day of greater reserve
available when the emergency occurs.
Before your 30-day challenge, I want to
give you a tool that works for any
surgical recommendation. I call it the
surgical clarity protocol. Five
questions, write them down and bring
them to any surgical consultation.
Question one, what is my estimated
surgical risk specifically? Not the
average for this procedure generally,
but my individual risk given my age, my
medical conditions, and my functional
status?
Question two, has my frailty been
formally assessed and if so, what does
that assessment suggest about my likely
recovery? Question three, what are the
realistic alternatives to surgery for my
specific condition and what does the
evidence show about how surgical
outcomes compared to non-surgical
management for a patient like me?
Question four, what does recovery
actually look like for someone my age
with my medical history? How long? What
level of functional limitation? What
rehabilitation is required? And what is
the realistic probability of returning
to my current level of independence?
Question five, if I choose not to have
the surgery or to delay it, what are the
specific consequences and is there a
time window within which surgery remains
an option if I decide to proceed later?
Any surgeon who is practicing
patient-centered medicine will engage
with these questions. They are not
challenges to surgical competence. They
are requests for the information that
allows an informed decision. And if a
surgeon responds to these questions with
impatience or dismissiveness, seek a
second opinion. You have that right and
exercising it is not a sign of distrust.
It is a sign of appropriate engagement
with a high-stakes decision. Here is
your 30-day action step, and for this
topic, it is specifically about
preparation because the most important
thing you can do for surgical outcomes
is to improve the physiological reserve
you bring to any operation before it
happens. Starting this week, choose one
thing from each of these three
categories and commit to it for 30 days.
In the nutrition category, add a
complete protein source to every meal,
eggs, fish, poultry, legumes, or dairy.
Adequate protein intake is one of the
most well-documented modifiable
predictors of surgical recovery, and
most adults over 65 are not eating
enough. Write down your current
approximate daily protein intake today
and target a minimum of 1.0 to 1.2 g of
protein per kilogram of body weight per
day. In the physical activity category,
add 10 minutes of resistance exercise,
body weight squats, chair squats,
resistance band work three times per
week. Muscle mass is the primary
determinant of physiological reserve,
and even a modest increase in lean mass
over 30 days measurably improves
recovery capacity.
In the planning category, schedule a
conversation with your primary care
physician specifically about your
surgical risk profile and advance care
planning, not because surgery is
imminent, but because having that
conversation before an emergency means
the information is available when it is
needed most. At 30 days, you will have a
clearer picture of your nutritional
baseline, a small but real improvement
in your functional reserve, and a
conversation on record about your goals
and values in the event of a medical
emergency. That is not a minor thing.
That is the difference between being
prepared and being caught without time
to prepare. There is a difference
between medicine that treats the
anatomical problem and medicine that
protects the whole person navigating
that problem. After 60, those two things
are not always achieved by the same
intervention. The best surgeons I have
encountered over 21 years are the ones
who understand this, who weigh the
recovery as carefully as the operation,
who ask about functional goals as
carefully as they study the imaging, and
who are willing to recommend watchful
waiting or less invasive alternatives
when the evidence supports it. A
surgical recommendation is the beginning
of a conversation. You now know what
that conversation should include. You
know what questions to ask. You know
what the evidence says about frailty,
recovery, and the gap between what
surgery promises and what it delivers in
patients whose physiological reserve is
not what it once was. You are not
powerless in front of a surgical
recommendation. You are a person with
the right to a full, honest,
evidence-based conversation about what
that recommendation means for you
specifically, and the questions to make
sure that conversation actually happens.
In 21 years, the patients I have watched
navigate surgical decisions most
successfully were almost never the ones
who simply agreed to everything. They
were the ones who asked the right
questions, understood the recovery as
clearly as the operation, and made
decisions that reflected their own
values and goals, not just the
anatomical finding on a scan. That is
the kind of patient you can be. And now
you have the tools to do it. If this
gave you something useful today,
subscribe. That is what this channel is
built for. Calm, honest, science-based
guidance for adults who want to
understand their health care, not just
receive it. The Longevity Guide is
linked in the description below. Share
this video with someone facing a
surgical decision who deserves to have
this conversation before signing the
consent form. I'll see you in the next
one.

Simple, trackable, and the evidence

statement means for you specifically at
your age with your history. That's not
what the science calls for, and it's not
what I've seen in 21 years as adequate
for the people I care about most in my
work. You have every right to understand
exactly what your two numbers mean, what
the gap between them is telling you, and
whether the conditions under which they
were measured actually reflect what's
happening in your body. Start today with
a correctly obtained reading and a
calculated pulse pressure. That's
genuinely all it takes to begin a better
conversation. If this gave you something
useful, go ahead and subscribe. That's
exactly what this channel is built for.
Calm, honest, science-based guidance
without the extremes you see everywhere
else online. And don't forget the
longevity guide linked below if you want
a structured daily plan to go alongside
everything we've covered today. I'll see
you in the next one.

Picture this. You're 67 years old. You
feel fine. Not perfect, but fine. Your
energy is decent, you're sleeping okay,
and life is pretty much on track. You go
in for a routine checkup. Nothing
dramatic, just one of those visits where
they run the usual panel. Your doctor
glances at your results and says, "Your
blood sugar is a little high. Let's
start watching your diet." So, you do
what most people do. You cut carbs. You
stop eating bread. You give up pasta.
You feel deprived for 3 weeks. You slip
back into old habits, and 6 months later
your blood sugar is exactly where it was
or higher. That story isn't unusual. I
hear some version of it almost every
week. And what makes it frustrating
isn't the intention behind the advice,
it's that the advice was incomplete.
Cutting carbohydrates is one approach to
blood sugar management. It is not the
only one, and for many people over 60,
it may not even be the most sustainable
long-term strategy. My name is Dr.
William Parker. I've spent 21 years
working in senior health, and this
channel exists for one reason: to give
you the research in plain language, so
you can make better decisions about your
own body before a condition gets ahead
of you. Today, we're talking about blood
sugar, specifically about 10 foods that
have been shown in clinical research to
improve your body's response to insulin,
slow glucose absorption, reduce
inflammation, and help your cells use
blood sugar the way they're supposed to.
These aren't wellness trends with
inflated claims. They're foods with real
mechanisms and published evidence behind
them. Stay with me through all 10,
because number eight is the one most
people have never considered in this
context, and the last one on this list
genuinely changes the conversation.
Before we get into the specifics, I need
to give you one concept. I call it the
glucose response lens. Without it, the
10 foods I'm about to share will feel
like a random grocery list. With it,
they'll make complete sense. Here's what
happens in your body when insulin
resistance takes hold, three things
specifically. First, your cells stop
listening. Insulin is the key that
unlocks the door to your cells so
glucose can enter and be used as energy.
When cells become insulin resistant,
those locks get stiff. The key is there,
it's turning, but the door won't open.
So, glucose stays in your bloodstream
instead. Second, your liver gets
confused. In a healthy body, insulin
signals the liver to stop releasing
stored sugar into the blood. In an
insulin-resistant body, that signal gets
ignored. Your liver keeps releasing
glucose even when blood sugar is already
elevated. It's like pouring water into a
glass that's already full. Third, and
this is the one most people never hear
about, chronic low-grade inflammation
makes everything worse. Inflammation
directly damages the insulin receptors
on your cells. The more inflamed your
system is, the less responsive those
receptors become. And here's the
cascade. High blood sugar triggers more
inflammation, which triggers more
insulin resistance, which keeps blood
sugar high. One feeds the other quietly
for years. So, here's the important
shift in thinking. If inflammation is
driving insulin resistance and insulin
resistance is keeping blood sugar
elevated, then foods that reduce
inflammation and improve receptor
function are just as important as foods
that simply slow sugar absorption.
That's the lens. Keep it in mind as we
go through each one. Now, I want to ask
you something. Think back 5 or 10 years.
Do you remember when you could eat a
full meal and feel steady an hour later?
When your energy didn't dip hard in the
afternoon? When you woke up clear-headed
without that foggy, heavy feeling? Most
people I speak with remember that. They
just assumed it was age. They assumed
things slowing down was simply part of
the picture. If any of that sounds
familiar, this video was made
specifically for you. Here's what I need
you to understand before we go further.
What you're experiencing is not your
body failing, it's your body responding
to inputs that can be changed. The
research on this is remarkably
consistent. Insulin sensitivity is not
fixed. It responds to what you eat, when
you eat it, and how consistently you
move. The adjustments, most of them are
far simpler than the advice most people
receive. Before we go deeper, if you
want a structured step-by-step guide
that maps everything we cover on this
channel into a daily plan, I've put
together a free longevity guide linked
in the description. Thousands of people
in this community are already using it.
Go ahead and grab it now while we work
through this together. Now, let's talk
about what's actually happening in your
body. When you eat carbohydrates, your
digestive system breaks them down into
glucose.
That glucose enters your bloodstream.
Your pancreas responds by releasing
insulin. Normally, insulin escorts
glucose into your muscle cells, your fat
cells, and your liver, where it gets
used or stored. That's the system
working correctly. When insulin
resistance develops, your cells stop
responding efficiently to insulin
signal. Your pancreas compensates by
producing more and more insulin, trying
to force the door open. For a while it
works. But over time, the pancreas gets
tired. Glucose starts accumulating in
the blood, and you end up with
chronically elevated blood sugar, even
if you're not eating anything
particularly extreme. The critical
insight is this: the solution is not
always to eat less glucose. Often, the
solution is to make your cells more
receptive to insulin again, reduce the
inflammation that's jamming the locks,
and slow the rate at which glucose
enters the bloodstream in the first
place. Now that you understand why this
happens, let me show you what actually
changes it. Multiple meta-analyses of
randomized controlled trials
consistently show that specific dietary
interventions, not just overall calorie
restriction, but specific foods can
meaningfully improve insulin sensitivity
in adults with pre-diabetes and type 2
diabetes. That's not a trend, that's
physiology responding to input, and it
changes how we have to think about
managing blood sugar. I rank 10 foods
from important to most critical so you
know exactly where to focus first. And
the last one on this list is the piece
most people overlook even when they're
doing everything else right. But it only
lands once you understand what comes
before it, so stay with me. Number one,
fenugreek seeds. Think of someone you
might know, maybe it's even you who has
been told for 2 years that blood sugar
is borderline. They've tried cutting
bread, walking more, nothing has moved
the needle. And nobody has ever
mentioned fenugreek. Most people think
of fenugreek, if they think of it at
all, as a cooking spice. That's not the
full picture. Fenugreek seeds contain a
compound called 4-hydroxyisoleucine,
which has a direct effect on insulin
secretion. They're also extraordinarily
high in soluble fiber, which forms a
gel-like substance in your gut, and
physically slows the rate at which
carbohydrates are absorbed into your
bloodstream. Think of it like a speed
bump between your meal and your blood
sugar spike. A 2023 meta-analysis
published in the International Journal
of Molecular Sciences pooled data from
10 randomized controlled trials and
found that fenugreek supplementation
significantly reduced fasting blood
glucose with a mean reduction of roughly
26 mg/dL
across studies compared to control
groups. That's a meaningful number, and
it comes from consistent daily use. The
practical approach, soak 1 tsp of
fenugreek seeds in a glass of water
overnight. Drink the water and eat the
seeds first thing in the morning before
food. The most common mistake people
make is using fenugreek powder in
cooking and expecting the same effect.
The soaking method releases the active
compounds far more reliably. One
important note, if you're currently on
diabetes medication, please speak with
your doctor before adding fenugreek to
your routine. It can enhance the
glucose-lowering effect of those
medications, and that combination needs
to be monitored. This is not medical
advice. Your doctor knows your full
picture. Number two, Ceylon cinnamon.
And I want to be specific here because
the type matters.
Think of the person who heard cinnamon
was good for blood sugar and has been
sprinkling it on their oatmeal every
morning for months, using the wrong kind
and getting little of the benefit. Most
cinnamon sold in grocery stores is
cassia cinnamon. It contains a compound
called coumarin that in large amounts
can stress the liver. Cassia cinnamon,
sometimes called true cinnamon, labeled
Cinnamomum verum, contains far less
coumarin and has a different active
compound called cinnamaldehyde.
Cinnamaldehyde improves how insulin
receptors function on the surface of
your cells. It helps the key fit the
lock better. A 2013 meta-analysis
published in the Annals of Family
Medicine, the same journal that
published the Allen review, analyzed 10
randomized controlled trials and found
that cinnamon supplementation
was associated with a statistically
significant reduction in fasting plasma
glucose of approximately 24 mg/dL
compared to control. It's worth noting
there is meaningful variability across
studies, and the effect appears
strongest in people with type 2 diabetes
versus prediabetes. Half a teaspoon to 1
tsp of Ceylon cinnamon daily is the
studied dose range. Stirred into warm
water, added to plain yogurt, or mixed
into oatmeal. Look specifically for the
label that says Ceylon or Cinnamomum
verum. The standard grocery variety does
not carry the same benefit profile and
poses a real risk to the liver at daily
doses. Quick pause here. Has your doctor
ever talked to you specifically about
foods that affect insulin sensitivity?
Drop a comment below. You would be
surprised how many people in this
community have been given a blood sugar
warning and received almost no dietary
guidance beyond watch the carbs. You're
not alone in that. Number three,
broccoli sprouts. Think of the person
who exercises, keeps their portions
reasonable, and still can't get their
blood sugar stable. The missing piece
they haven't heard of yet is
sulforaphane. Most people think of
broccoli as just a healthy vegetable.
What they may not know is that the
sprout form, the tiny seedlings you can
find in some grocery stores or grow at
home, contains up to 100 times more
sulforaphane
than mature brocc. Sulforaphane is a
compound that activates a cellular
pathway called NRF2, which reduces
oxidative stress and directly decreases
liver glucose production. Remember the
second truth from our lens, the liver
releasing too much glucose even when
blood sugar is already high.
Sulforaphane helps correct that specific
problem. A double-blind,
placebo-controlled study published in
Science Translational Medicine in 2017
by Axelsson and colleagues followed
obese participants with type 2 diabetes
who were not well controlled on standard
medication and found that concentrated
sulforaphane from broccoli sprout
extract reduced fasting blood sugar by
roughly 10% over 12 weeks without any
other dietary changes. Two to three
tablespoons of fresh broccoli sprouts on
a salad or sandwich daily is a
low-effort way to access this mechanism.
The most common mistake is cooking them.
Heat destroys sulforaphane. Eat them
raw. Number four, avocado. And this one
works through a mechanism most people
don't associate with blood sugar at all.
Think of the person avoiding avocado
because they've heard it's too high in
fat. The fat in avocado is precisely
what their blood sugar management is
missing. The monounsaturated fat in
avocado, primarily oleic acid, slows
gastric emptying, meaning food leaves
your stomach more gradually, which means
glucose enters your bloodstream more
slowly. That prevents the sharp
post-meal spikes that exhaust your
insulin response. Avocados are also rich
in magnesium, and chronically low
magnesium levels are one of the more
consistent findings in people with
insulin resistance. A randomized
controlled study published in the
Journal of Nutrition in 2021 found that
adults who added half an avocado to
their daily diet showed significantly
reduced post-meal glucose response and
improved markers of insulin sensitivity
compared to the control group over a
12-week period. Half an avocado daily
with eggs in a salad or simply with a
little salt matches the study dose.
The mistake most people make is treating
avocado as an occasional indulgence
rather than a consistent daily tool.
Number five, chia seeds. Think of
someone who's heard chia seeds are good
for something, started adding them to
smoothies, and hasn't noticed much. The
issue isn't the food, it's the form.
Chia seeds are one of the most
concentrated sources of soluble fiber
available in any whole food. When they
absorb liquid, and they absorb up to 12
times their weight in water, they form a
gel. That gel sitting in your digestive
tract physically slows carbohydrate
absorption. It also reduces the glycemic
response to everything else you eat
alongside it. Chia seeds don't just slow
their own digestion, they slow the
digestion of the entire meal. Multiple
randomized trials have confirmed that
chia seeds reduce post-meal blood sugar
spikes significantly when added to high
glycemic meals, with some studies
showing reductions of roughly 35 to 40%
compared to the same meal without chia.
2 Tbsp per day is the practical dose.
Soak them in water for about 20 minutes
before eating. This activates the gel
before they enter your gut, which
significantly improves the effect. The
mistake most people make is eating them
dry, which slows their action and limits
the fiber benefit. All right, everything
up to this point has been important, but
what I'm about to share now is where the
real conversation begins. These are the
foods that people come back to me about,
the ones they say changed how they
actually feel day-to-day. Pay close
attention. Number six, fatty fish. Think
of the person who has been managing
borderline blood sugar for 3 years and
cut their saturated fat intake
significantly. What they haven't done is
replace it with the right fats. Most
people think of omega-3 fatty acids in
terms of heart health. The connection to
blood sugar is equally important, but
far less discussed. Omega-3s,
specifically EPA and DHA, found in fatty
fish like salmon, mackerel, and
sardines, reduce inflammatory cytokines
throughout the body. Remember truth
number three from our lens, chronic
inflammation damages insulin receptors.
Omega-3s directly work against that
damage, helping restore the receptor
function that insulin resistance has
degraded. A systematic review published
in Diabetes Care analyzed multiple
controlled trials and found that regular
omega-3 intake from fish sources
significantly reduced inflammatory
markers associated with insulin
resistance.
Within two to three weeks of consistent
fatty fish consumption, most people
notice improved energy steadiness after
meals, less of that hard mid-afternoon
crash, Two to three servings per week of
wild caught salmon, mackerel, or
sardines delivers a meaningful dose of
EPA and DHA. The mistake most people
make is relying entirely on fish oil
capsules without eating whole fish. The
broader nutrient profile of whole food
sources appears to support the
anti-inflammatory effect more
completely. Number seven, walnuts. Think
of someone who has been told to avoid
nuts because of calorie density. What
wasn't mentioned is that walnuts have a
metabolic profile that looks very
different from their calorie count
suggests. Walnuts are the only common
nut that provides meaningful amounts of
alpha-linolenic acid, the plant-based
omega-3. They also contain polyphenols,
antioxidant compounds that reduce
oxidative stress in the pancreatic beta
cells responsible for producing insulin.
When those cells are under chronic
oxidative stress, insulin output
declines. Walnuts help protect that
output. A prospective study from the
Harvard School of Public Health, the
Nurses' Health Study, which followed
nearly 138,000
women over 10 years found that consuming
two or more servings of walnuts per week
was associated with a roughly 33% lower
risk of developing type 2 diabetes
compared to those who rarely or never
ate them. That's an observational
finding, not a controlled trial, so it
shows association rather than direct
cause. But combined with the biological
mechanism, it's a compelling picture.
One ounce, about seven whole walnuts, is
one serving. Eat them as a between-meal
snack or add them to oatmeal or salad.
The mistake most people make is buying
flavored or honey-roasted versions,
which add sugar and directly undermine
the benefit. Plain raw walnuts are what
the evidence supports. Number eight,
eggs. And this one genuinely surprises
people. Think of someone who has been
avoiding eggs for 10 years because of
cholesterol concerns. They may be
missing one of the most effective blood
sugar stabilizing foods available at
breakfast. I want to be clear here. This
is not medical advice, and if you have
specific concerns about cholesterol,
please discuss them with your own
physician because individual
circumstances vary. But here's what the
blood sugar research shows. Eggs are
among the most satiating foods
available. Their protein and fat
combination suppresses the post-meal
hormonal signals that drive blood sugar
and hunger spikes.
They also contain choline, which
supports liver function. And as we've
covered, the liver plays a direct role
in blood sugar regulation. A randomized
controlled trial published in the
American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
followed adults with type 2 diabetes
over 12 weeks and found that those who
ate two eggs at breakfast showed
significantly improved fasting blood
sugar and greater insulin sensitivity by
the end of the study compared to those
eating a high-carbohydrate breakfast.
Two eggs, soft-boiled, poached, or
scrambled without added sugars is the
practical dose. The mistake most people
make is pairing them with high glycemic
sides like toast or juice, which cancels
much of the blood sugar benefit the eggs
themselves provide. Number nine, apple
cider vinegar. Think of someone who
dismissed apple cider vinegar as a
wellness trend. They were right to be
skeptical of the more extreme claims
that circulate online, but wrong to
dismiss the actual mechanism, which is
well documented. The acetic acid in
apple cider vinegar inhibits the enzyme
that breaks starches down into glucose.
Slow that enzyme and you slow glucose
absorption. Acetic acid also appears to
improve insulin signaling in muscle
cells, which supports the uptake of
glucose after a meal. The evidence here
comes from a 2004 study by Johnston and
colleagues published in Diabetes Care,
which found that taking 2 Tbsp of
vinegar before a high carbohydrate meal
improved insulin sensitivity by between
19 and 34% in insulin-resistant adults.
A real published result from a credible
journal. The effect is most pronounced
when taken before the highest
carbohydrate meal of the day. 2 tsp to 2
Tbsp diluted in a full glass of water
about 10 minutes before that meal is the
studied protocol. The mistake most
people make is drinking it undiluted,
which can damage tooth enamel and
irritate the esophagus over time. Always
dilute it.
And if you have a history of acid reflux
or gastroparesis, speak with your doctor
before adding this. And now, number 10.
Here it is, the one that changes the
conversation entirely.
Lentils. Think of someone who has done
almost everything right. They've added
several of the foods from this list.
They're walking daily, their blood sugar
improved, but then it plateaued. They
can't figure out what's missing. What's
missing is the starch baseline. Here is
something most people never hear. It's
not just about what you add to your
diet. It's about what those additions
replace. And when it comes to blood
sugar management, lentils are the most
powerful starch replacement most people
have never seriously considered. Lentils
have a glycemic index of roughly 29
compared to 70 for white bread and 56
for white rice. They are extraordinarily
high in resistant starch, a type of
carbohydrate that passes through the
small intestine without being digested
and instead feeds beneficial gut
bacteria in the colon. Those bacteria
produce short-chain fatty acids that
directly improve insulin sensitivity at
the cellular level. Lentils are also
high in soluble fiber, protein, and
magnesium, three nutrients that
independently support blood sugar
regulation. a randomized controlled
trial by Jenkins and colleagues at the
University of Toronto, published in the
Archives of Internal Medicine in 2012,
followed 121 participants with type 2
diabetes over 3 months. The group that
replaced high glycemic staple foods with
legumes, including lentils, showed a
significant reduction in HbA1c, key
long-term blood sugar marker, as well as
reduced cardiovascular risk scores
compared to those eating high-fiber
wheat products. The legume group also
saw meaningful blood pressure
improvements. What that means for you is
that replacing even one serving of white
rice or white bread with half a cup of
cooked lentils per day addresses your
starch baseline in a way that no
supplement or add-on food can match. And
here is why most people never get there.
They do everything else and leave this
one out. They add vinegar before meals.
They take cinnamon. They eat more fish,
but the staple starch they eat every day
never changes. Lentils change the starch
baseline. You don't need to overhaul
your entire diet. Start two or three
times per week. Add them to soups. Use
them as a side dish. Put them under your
protein instead of rice.
Within a month, most people who make
this swap consistently report steadier
energy, reduced afternoon fatigue, and
measurable improvement in how they feel
after meals. Before I give you your
30-day challenge, I want to leave you
with something practical you can use at
your very next appointment. I call it
the blood sugar clarity protocol. Five
questions that will help you have a far
more productive conversation with your
physician. First, what is my current
fasting blood sugar and A1c, and where
specifically do you want those numbers
to be in 6 months? Get specific targets,
not just better. Second, are any of the
medications I'm currently taking known
to affect blood sugar or insulin
sensitivity. Many common medications
including certain blood pressure drugs
and corticosteroids can raise blood
sugar. You deserve to know if that's a
factor in your numbers. Third, what
specific dietary changes would have the
most impact for someone with my numbers
right now? Push for specifics, not just
watch the sugar.
Fourth, at what point would we consider
medication if my numbers don't improve
and what would that process look like?
Understand the timeline before you're in
it. Fifth, beyond fasting glucose and a
1C, are there tests that would give us a
more complete picture of my insulin
function?
Fasting insulin levels and the HOMA-IR
score can identify insulin resistance
before A1C becomes abnormal. Not every
physician orders these routinely.
Knowing to ask is genuinely useful. Any
good physician will welcome these
questions and if they don't, that itself
tells you something important. Here is
your 30-day challenge. Choose three of
the 10 foods from today's list that you
don't currently eat regularly. Add one
of them to your daily routine this week.
Add the second one the week after.
The third in week three, in week four
focus on consistency, not perfection.
Write down your fasting blood sugar
today if you have a home monitor or
simply note how your energy feels in the
hour after your main meal.
Check again at the end of 30 days. Three
foods added gradually, tracked simply.
The difference at 30 days will surprise
you. I want to close with something I
think about a lot after 21 years in this
work. There is a difference between
health care that generates findings and
health care that protects your quality
of life. A blood sugar number is a
finding. How you feel at 2:00 in the
afternoon, whether you have the energy
to do what matters to you, whether
you're sharp and steady and present,
that's quality of life. The best
physicians I've ever known understand
that those two goals are not always the
same, and they never sacrifice one for
the other without a conversation. You
have probably been told that rising
blood sugar is just part of getting
older, that your body is simply slowing
down, that this is what it looks like
from here. That is not what the science
consistently shows, and it is not what
I've seen in 21 years of working with
people who decided to approach this
differently. You are not broken. You are
not past the point of meaningful change.
You have the right to understand what's
happening in your body, why it's
happening, and what the evidence
actually supports. The 10 foods we
covered today are not a cure, and they
are not medical advice. They are tools,
real researched practical tools that you
can begin using this week. Talk to your
doctor about the ones most relevant to
your situation. Start with one. Start
today. That is all it takes. If this
gave you something useful, subscribe.
That is what this channel is built for,
calm, real, science-based guidance
without the extremes, without the fear,
without the condescension. The Longevity
Guide is linked in the description. Grab
it, use it, and share it with someone
who could use this information. I'll see
you in the next one.

Are you over 70? Some routine medical screening tests may not always provide the same benefits they once did. In this video, learn about 5 common screening tests seniors should discuss with their doctor before agreeing to them automatically. Discover the latest evidence on preventive care, healthy aging, colonoscopy after 75, PSA testing, mammograms, heart stress tests, bone density scans, and carotid artery screening.

You'll learn why the balance between benefits and risks changes with age, how unnecessary testing can lead to more procedures, and the important questions every older adult should ask before any medical screening. This video is designed to help seniors make informed healthcare decisions with their doctor.

In this video:
• 5 medical screening tests seniors should review after age 70
• Colonoscopy after 75 explained
• Mammogram and PSA screening for older adults
• Heart stress tests without symptoms
• Bone density scans and osteoporosis treatment
• Carotid artery ultrasound risks and benefits
• Questions to ask your doctor before any screening
• Healthy aging and evidence-based senior healthcare tips

If you found this video helpful, Like, Subscribe, and Share with your family and friends so they can make informed healthcare decisions too.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult your physician or another qualified healthcare professional before making decisions about medical tests, screenings, treatments, or medications. Healthcare recommendations vary based on your age, medical history, and overall health.

Most people believe that more medical
testing is always better. That more
screening means more safety. That
finding something early is always the
right move. That belief is
understandable. It's what we've been
taught and for many tests at many ages
it is absolutely true. But after 70
something shifts and the shift is not
subtle. The same screening tests that
protect a 55-year-old can in certain
circumstances trigger
of procedures in a 75-year-old
that causes more harm than the condition
they were looking for. Not because the
tests are bad, not because the doctors
ordering them are wrong, but because the
math of benefit and risk changes as we
age and most patients are never told
that the math has changed. The US
Preventive Services Task Force, the
independent body of physicians and
scientists that evaluates evidence on
preventive care, has published guidance
suggesting that several routine
screening tests commonly performed in
older adults either provide diminishing
benefit, carry increasing procedural
risk or both after certain age
thresholds. These recommendations are
not fringe opinions. They are
evidence-based conclusions from some of
the most rigorous medical review panels
in the country. And yet most patients
over 70 are still receiving these tests
automatically without a personalized
conversation about whether the benefits
still outweighs the risk for them
specifically. My name is Dr. William
Parker. I have spent 21 years
specializing in senior health and today
I want to have that conversation with
you. I am going to walk you through five
screening tests that deserve a more
careful personalized discussion after
age 70. What the evidence actually
shows, what the risks are and what
questions you should be asking your
physician before you agree to them
automatically. I want to be clear about
something before we begin. This is not a
video telling you to refuse medical
care. It is a video about informed
consent, about your right to understand
what a test is actually likely to do for
you, specifically at your age, with your
health history, before you agree to it.
That is a right every patient has, and
it is one that too few people exercise.
Stay with me through all five. Screening
number four is the one most people never
question, and it is the one where the
gap between perceived benefit
and actual benefit is widest for older
adults. And screening number five
reframes the entire conversation about
what preventive medicine after 70 should
actually be for. If this channel is new
to you, subscribe now. This is what we
do here, calm, evidence-based guidance
for adults who want to understand their
health care, not just receive it. Let's
get into it. Before I walk you through
the five screenings, I need to give you
one framework. Without it, the
individual examples won't connect into a
principle you can use. I call it the
age-shifted calculus, and it changes how
you think about every medical
recommendation you receive after 70.
Three things change about the
benefit-risk calculation for screening
tests as we age. First, the lead time
shrinks. Screening tests find things
early so that treatment can begin while
there is still time to meaningfully
change the outcome.
At 55, finding a slow-growing cancer
early might add 15 or 20 years of
healthy life. At 78, the same early
detection might add months, or in some
cases produce no survival benefit at
all, while still exposing the patient to
the anxiety, procedures, and
complications that follow a positive
result. The lead time that makes
screening valuable compresses
significantly after a certain age.
Second, procedural risk rises. A
colonoscopy in a healthy 55-year-old
carries a very low complication rate.
The same procedure in a 78-year-old on
multiple medications with reduced kidney
function and age-related changes in
bowel wall tissue carries a meaningfully
different risk profile. The procedure
didn't change, the patient did. Third,
and this is the one most patients never
hear clearly stated, the cascade effect
becomes more dangerous.
One positive test almost never ends the
conversation. It begins one One test
leads to a follow-up. A follow-up leads
to a biopsy. A biopsy leads to a
treatment decision. At each step, a
person who walked in feeling completely
fine is now managing risk, side effects,
anxiety, and complications from a
process that may have been triggered by
finding something that was never going
to harm them. The older the patient, the
harder the body recovers from each step
in that cascade. That is the age-shifted
calculus. It is the filter for
everything that follows. Keep it with I
want to ask you something.
Think back to the last time you left a
routine appointment with a new test
ordered. Did you ask why? Did you ask
what would happen if the result came
back abnormal and what the step after
that would be?
Most people don't, not because they're
passive, but because they trust the
system. And for most of their lives,
that trust has been well placed. But at
some point in the 70s, the automatic
checklist that was protected at 60
deserves a different kind of
conversation. Not suspicion, just a more
personalized one. If you've ever had a
test lead to another test or a finding
lead to a procedure and quietly wondered
afterward whether all of it was
necessary, this video was made for you.
Here is what I want you to hold on to.
Questioning a screening test is not the
same as refusing medical care. Asking
your physician, "Why is this right for
me specifically at my age?" is one of
the most medically responsible things
you can do. It leads to better
conversations, more personalized
decisions, and in many cases better
outcomes. Before we go deeper, if you
want a written guide that helps you
organize these conversations, my free
longevity guide is linked in the
description below. Grab it now and
follow along. Let me explain the
mechanism that makes the cascade effect
specifically risky for older adults
because once you see it clearly, each of
the five screenings will make immediate
sense. Picture a single pebble dropped
into still water. It creates rings that
spread outward, each one a consequence
of the first impact. In medicine, a
positive screening result is that
pebble. The rings are the subsequent
tests, procedures, and treatment
decisions that follow almost
automatically. For a younger, healthier
patient, those rings spread across calm
water. Each one is manageable, the body
recovers between them. The kidneys, the
cardiovascular system, the immune
response, they absorb the stress of
procedures and bounce back. For an older
patient managing multiple chronic
conditions, taking multiple medications
with age-related changes in organ
function and healing capacity, the water
is not as calm. The rings interact. A
biopsy requiring anesthesia interacts
with kidney function. A new medication
started after a finding interacts with
medications already being taken. A
period of restricted activity following
a procedure accelerates the muscle loss
in someone already at the margin. This
is not a reason to avoid all medical
intervention. It is a reason to be
deliberate about which pebble you drop
and when. The American Board of Internal
Medicine's Choosing Wisely initiative,
in which dozens of specialty
organizations have published
recommendations about tests and
treatments that are commonly ordered but
not always necessary.
Includes multiple screening tests in its
guidance for older adults. The unifying
principle, the value of any medical
intervention must be weighed against its
burden. And that calculation is
individual, not universal.
Now, the five screenings I have ordered
them from common and frequently
misunderstood to most significant
because the final one reframes
everything else on the list. Screening
one, routine colonoscopy after age 75.
Leonard was 77. He had been having
colonoscopies every 10 years since he
turned 50. His most recent one, 3 years
earlier, was completely clean. His
internist ordered another one as
routine. Leonard didn't question it. He
assumed it was still the right thing. He
went in for the bowel preparation the
day before. The large volume of laxative
solution required caused a significant
electrolyte imbalance. And Leonard ended
up in the emergency room for 2 days
before the procedure even happened. Most
people think of colonoscopy as low risk.
For most adults under 70, that is
largely accurate. For adults over 75,
the risk profile is different in three
specific ways. The bowel preparation
involves large volumes of liquid and
powerful laxatives over 24 hours. In
younger patients, the dehydration and
electrolyte shifts this causes are minor
and self-correcting. In older patients,
particularly those on diuretics, blood
pressure medications, or with any degree
of kidney impairment, these shifts can
be clinically significant. The sedation
required for the procedure carries
elevated risk in patients with
cardiovascular or pulmonary conditions.
And the bowel wall itself becomes
thinner and more fragile with age,
increasing the risk of perforation
during the scope. The US Preventive
Services Task Force recommends that
colorectal cancer screening continue
through age 75 for most patients, that
the decision to screen between ages 76
and 85 be individualized, and that after
age 85 the harms of screening likely
outweigh the benefits.
Research published in JAMA Internal
Medicine found that among adults age 70
and older with a prior negative
colonoscopy, the probability of
developing colorectal cancer within 10
years was low, while the procedural
complication rate was not negligible.
The practical guidance, if you are over
75, have had a recent clean colonoscopy,
and are being scheduled for another one
automatically, ask your physician
specifically, given my age, my prior
screening history, and my current
health, what is the specific benefit I'm
likely to get from this procedure? And
how does that compare to the preparation
and procedural risks for someone my age?
That is not a refusal, it is a request
for individualized reasoning, and you
are fully entitled to it. The common
mistake is assuming that because a test
has always been ordered, it still
carries the same rationale it always
did. The test didn't change, your
circumstances did. The next screening
involves a more emotionally charged
question, because the word cancer
changes how most people think about
risk. Screening two, aggressive cancer
screening, mammograms and PSA prostate
testing after age 75. Alice was 76. She
had been getting annual mammograms since
her early 50s. Her most recent one
showed a small finding that required
further imaging. That imaging led to a
biopsy. The biopsy found a very small,
slow-growing tumor. She underwent a
lumpectomy followed by 6 weeks of
radiation. The recovery was long and
hard. A year later her oncologist
mentioned that the tumor had features
suggesting it was so slow-growing that
it likely would never have caused
symptoms or affected her lifespan. But
once it was found, the medical and
emotional momentum of the cascade had
made stopping at any step feel
unthinkable.
The concept at the center of this
conversation is called overdiagnosis.
Finding a cancer that would never have
become clinically significant during the
patient's remaining lifetime. This is
not a theoretical concern. It is a
documented phenomenon in cancer
screening literature and its frequency
increases with age because slower
growing cancers make up a larger
proportion of findings in older patients
and competing causes of death become
more relevant. The US Preventive
Services Task Force recommends that
mammography screening decisions in women
75 and older be individualized, citing
insufficient evidence that continued
screening benefits this age group while
acknowledging documented harms from
false positives and overtreatment. For
PSA prostate cancer screening, the task
force recommends against routine
screening in men 70 and older, citing
evidence that the harms of detection and
treatment, including incontinence,
erectile dysfunction, and cardiovascular
effects from some hormonal treatments
outweigh the benefits for most men in
this age group. A major analysis
published in the New England Journal of
Medicine estimated that among men
diagnosed with prostate cancer through
PSA screening, a substantial proportion
had cancers that would never have caused
symptoms or death, but the treatments
those men received caused real lasting
harm. The practical guidance, if you are
being scheduled for routine mammography
over age 75 or if a PSA test is being
ordered as part of your annual panel,
ask your physician, "Given my age and
overall health, what is the realistic
benefit of finding something through
this test, and what would the treatment
path actually look like for the most
likely finding?" The answer to that
second question is the one most people
never receive before agreeing to the
test. The common mistake is equating
detection with protection. Finding
something is only protective when acting
on it meaningfully improves your quality
or length of life.
At 75 and beyond, that equation requires
a specific answer for your specific
situation. Quick pause, has a physician
ever had a specific conversation with
you about whether a routine screening
was still appropriate for your age, or
has it simply always been scheduled as
part of your annual visit? Drop a yes or
no in the comments. This conversation is
rarer than it should be, and the people
in this community deserve to know
they're not alone in never having had
it. Screening three, routine cardiac
stress testing in people without
symptoms. George was 73. He felt
completely well. His annual executive
health panel included a cardiac stress
test as it always had. The test showed
an abnormality. He was referred for a
cardiac catheterization. The
catheterization found a narrowing in one
coronary artery. He was placed on a
stent. He experienced a complication at
the vascular access site and required an
additional hospitalization. Several
years later, his cardiologist
acknowledged that given his complete
absence of symptoms, the evidence
suggested that optimal medical
management alone without the procedure
would have achieved the same
cardiovascular outcome while avoiding
the procedural risk entirely. The
ischemia trial, published in the New
England Journal of Medicine in 2020,
followed over 5,000 patients with
moderate to severe coronary artery
disease and found that an initial
invasive strategy, stenting or bypass
surgery, did not reduce the risk of
heart attack or death compared to
optimal medical management alone in
patients who were clinically stable and
without significant symptoms. For stable
asymptomatic patients, the cascade
triggered by finding a blockage did not
produce better outcomes than careful
medical therapy. But, it did produce
procedural risk. In asymptomatic older
adults, routine stress testing follows
exactly this cascade pattern. An
abnormal result leads almost
automatically to catheterization.
Catheterization often leads to
intervention. And intervention in an
older patient carries risks,
contrast-induced kidney injury,
bleeding, arrhythmia, vascular
complications that in a symptomatic
patient may be clearly justified by
clinical need, but in an asymptomatic
patient require much more careful
individual consideration. The practical
guidance, if you feel well, have no
chest pain, no significant shortness of
breath with ordinary activity, and are
being scheduled for a routine cardiac
stress test without a specific clinical
reason, ask your physician what specific
symptom or finding is this test designed
to investigate, and what would we do
differently if the result is abnormal
versus normal? If the answer is, "It's
just routine," that is the right moment
to ask for a more specific justification
tied to your individual situation. The
common mistake is assuming that a test
recommended by a physician has already
been individualized. In busy clinical
settings, standard protocols often drive
test ordering more than individualized
patient assessment does.
Asking for the reasoning is not
challenging the physician's judgment. It
is inviting a better conversation. I
want to shift focus now. What comes next
is where the age-shifted calculus
applies most directly to daily quality
of life, and where I have seen the most
significant gap between what patients
are told and what the evidence actually
shows. Screening for routine bone
density DEXA scans and automatic
osteoporosis treatment initiation in
adults over 80. The fear driving this
screening is entirely legitimate. Hip
fractures in older adults are serious.
They carry real risks of functional
decline, hospitalization complications,
and in some cases significant mortality.
The desire to protect against them is
completely reasonable. What is worth
examining carefully is whether the
automatic pathway from low DEXA score to
medication initiation achieves what
patients and families hope it achieves,
particularly in the very elderly.
Margaret was 82. Her DEXA scan showed
low bone density. She was started on a
bisphosphonate medication and took it
faithfully for 5 years, experiencing
persistent gastrointestinal side effects
throughout. During a later consultation,
her physician noted that the evidence
for bisphosphonate benefit in women over
80 is considerably weaker than the
evidence in women in their 60s. And that
fall prevention interventions, removing
rugs and tripping hazards at home,
balance and strength training,
medication review for drugs that
increase fall risk, and vision
correction had strong consistent
evidence for reducing fracture rates at
any age and carried no medication side
effects whatsoever. These interventions
had never been offered to Margaret as a
primary strategy. The distinction the
research supports is clear. In adults
under 70 to 75 with osteoporosis,
medications to increase bone density has
solid evidence of fracture risk
reduction. In adults over 80, the
evidence thins and multiple professional
guidelines, including guidance from the
American Geriatrics Society, note that
the benefit-risk calculation is less
clear, particularly for patients who are
frail, managing multiple medications, or
who have had prior fractures. Meanwhile,
fall prevention interventions have
consistent, well-documented evidence at
every age and carry none of the
medication burden. The practical
guidance, if you are over 78 and being
started on osteoporosis medication
following a DEXA scan, or if you have
been on such medication for several
years, ask your physician, what is the
specific evidence for this medication
reducing fracture risk for someone my
age, and have we fully addressed the
fall prevention factors that are equally
or more important? Both conversations
belong in the room. Most of the time
only one of them happens. The common
mistake is treating the bone density
number as the only relevant variable. It
is a data point. The right treatment
decision requires context. Your age,
your functional status, your medication
burden, your fall history, and what you
want your daily life to look like. Now,
here it is, the screening that most
completely illustrates everything I have
been building toward, and the one that
carries the most significant procedural
risk when the cascade it triggers goes
wrong. Screening five, carotid artery
ultrasound in people without any
neurological symptoms. I want to be
precise here, because this screening has
an important and appropriate use, and I
want to distinguish that from the
context we're discussing today. When a
patient has experienced a TIA, a
transient ischemic attack, the kind of
warning event we covered in a prior
video, or any neurological symptoms
suggesting reduced blood flow to the
brain, imaging the carotid arteries is a
critical and clearly indicated step.
That is not what we're discussing. What
we are discussing is routine carotid
ultrasound screening in older adults
with no neurological symptoms
whatsoever. Simply a screening test
included in a cardiovascular panel, or
offered at a community health screening
event, or part of a comprehensive
preventive workup. Richard was 74, he
felt completely well. His physician
mentioned that given his age and
cardiovascular risk factors, a carotid
ultrasound might be worthwhile. The
ultrasound found a significant narrowing
of about 70% on one side. He was
referred to a vascular surgeon. Surgery
was recommended. Richard elected to
proceed. During the carotid
endarterectomy, a surgical procedure to
remove the buildup from the artery wall,
he had a stroke. The procedure intended
to prevent a stroke caused one.
This is not an extreme outlier. The
stroke risk of carotid endarterectomy in
asymptomatic patients runs in the range
of 2 to 3% across published surgical
literature. For a patient who is
symptomatic, who has already had a TIA
from that artery, that procedural risk
may be clearly justified by the risk the
untreated stenosis poses.
For a patient with no symptoms, the
justification requires much more careful
examination. The US Preventive Services
Task Force currently recommends against
screening for asymptomatic carotid
artery stenosis in the general adult
population, concluding that the harms,
driven primarily by the cascade
following a positive result, outweigh
the benefits for people with no
neurological symptoms. Research from the
Veterans Affairs Cooperative Studies
Program found that while surgery reduced
stroke risk in selected asymptomatic
patients over several years, the
absolute benefit was modest. And the
patients who benefited most were
younger, healthier, and at lower
procedural risk, a profile that often
does not describe the patients being
offered this screening at 75 or 80. What
the evidence does support at any age and
for any degree of carotid artery disease
is optimal medical management,
well-controlled blood pressure, lipid
management, antiplatelet therapy where
appropriate, and the lifestyle factors
that reduce cardiovascular risk across
the board. Multiple recent trials have
found that optimal medical therapy
achieves outcomes that approach or equal
surgical intervention for asymptomatic
patients without the procedural stroke
risk. The practical guidance if a
carotid ultrasound finding is presented
to you and surgery is raised as an
option, ask three specific questions
before proceeding. First, what is my
annual stroke risk from this finding
based on current evidence and how does
that compare to the procedural stroke
risk at this center? Second, what does
optimal medical management look like as
an alternative to surgery and what would
that involve specifically? Third, am I a
candidate who the evidence suggests
benefits from surgery or am I in a group
where the benefit over medical
management is less clear? Those three
questions reframe the conversation from
automatic cascade to informed individual
decision. That is exactly where it
belongs. The common mistake, and it is
the most consequential one on today's
entire list, is treating the discovery
of a finding as automatic justification
for the intervention that follows. It is
not. A finding requires evaluation.
Evaluation requires context and context
requires a physician willing to walk
through the evidence with you, not just
the referral pathway. Before your 30-day
action step, here is a tool for your
next appointment. I call it the
screening value clarity protocol. Five
questions, write them down.
They apply to any screening but are
especially valuable for the five we
covered today. Question one, what
specific benefit am I likely to get from
the screening at my age and with my
health history compared to the general
population this test was originally
designed for? Question two, if this test
comes back abnormal, what is the next
step and what is the step after that? I
want to understand the full cascade
before I agree to the first step.
Question three, what are the procedural
risks specific to me accounting for my
age, my current medications, and my
overall health status? Question four, is
there an evidence-based alternative to
the screening or it's likely follow-up
that I should understand before we
proceed? Question five, does the US
Preventive Services Task Force, the
American Geriatric Society, or any
relevant specialty organization have
guidance about whether this test is
recommended for someone my age
specifically? Any physician practicing
evidence-based patient-centered medicine
will welcome these questions.
Not as a challenge to their competence,
as an invitation to a better
conversation. And if the response is
dismissive of questions this reasonable,
that is information worth having about
your care. Here is your 30-day action
step. Before your next scheduled
appointment, write down every screening
test you have had in the past 3 years.
For each one, note how old you were when
you first started having it, and whether
anyone has ever had a specific
individualized conversation with you
about whether it still makes sense for
your age and current health. Bring that
list to your next appointment with one
sentence ready. I want to make sure the
tests I'm having are still the right
tests for where I am now. That sentence
does not challenge anyone.
It invites collaboration. And in 30
days, you will have had at least one
conversation about your health care that
did not happen automatically, one that
you initiated on your terms with the
right questions in hand.
There is a difference between medicine
that screens for everything that can be
found and medicine that focuses on what
will actually improve your quality and
length of life. After 70, those two
things diverge in ways that most
patients, and frankly many physicians
working under time pressure, do not
fully appreciate in the moment. The best
doctors I have known over 21 years are
not the ones who ordered the most tests.
They are the ones who ask the most
careful questions. Who understood that a
finding is only valuable when acting on
it makes a patient's life genuinely
better. Who had the intellectual
confidence to say, "For you specifically
at this point in your life, this test is
worth doing or this one isn't." That is
the medicine that serves people well
after 70. And now you have the framework
and the questions to help bring that
medicine into your own care. You are not
a checklist. You are a person with a
specific history, specific goals, and
specific priorities. And the health care
you receive should reflect all three.
In 21 years, I've watched patients who
ask better questions receive better
care. Not because they were difficult,
because the questions created space for
the right conversation, and that space
is yours to create. If this gave you
something useful, subscribe. That is
what this channel is built for, calm,
evidence-based guidance for adults who
want to understand their health care,
not just receive it. I'll see you in the
next one.

Could your salad be making you sick? A dangerous Cyclospora parasite outbreak has infected thousands of people across the United States, with investigators tracing many cases to contaminated shredded iceberg lettuce. But is lettuce really the problem, or is the real danger hidden in the water used to grow our food?

In this video, Dr. William Parker explains everything you need to know about the current Cyclospora outbreak, including the reported link to Taylor Farms, how the parasite spreads, the symptoms to watch for, who is most at risk, and the simple steps you can take to protect yourself and your family. You'll also learn why older adults, people with weak immune systems, and those with chronic health conditions should take this outbreak seriously.

This evidence based guide covers:

What Cyclospora is and how it spreads
The latest lettuce outbreak explained
Cyclospora symptoms and how long they last
Why contaminated irrigation water may be the real source
Foods to avoid during the outbreak
Safe fruits and vegetables to eat
Can washing lettuce remove Cyclospora?
Natural remedies: what works and what doesn't
When you should see a doctor
Simple food safety tips to reduce your risk

right now. Go ahead. Actually think

from? Not the grocery store you bought
it at before that. What farm? What water
was used to grow it? What water was used
to wash it before it ever got shredded
into a bag? Most of us have never once
asked that question because we've never
had a reason to. As of this month, over
1,600 people across the country now have
a very specific reason. There's a
multi-state outbreak happening right now
tied to a parasite most people have
never heard of called cycllospora. It's
been linked to iceberg lettuce supplied
by one of the largest produce companies
in the country served at a major
restaurant chain and the investigation
is still unfolding. Here's what makes
this different from ordinary food
poisoning. This organism won't make you
sick for 7 to 14 days after exposure.

common mistake is stopping when

controlled appropriate challenge.

If you have osteoporosis, recent joint
replacement, or cardiovascular concerns,

Sedentary adults over 70 lose ground
significantly faster than those who
engage in resistance training at any
level.

consistency, dimming lights and avoiding

68° F
as your core body temperature drops

Get these right and the whole system

attention here. This is where the real

protein, and specifically how you

been. After 70, your muscle protein
synthesis, your body's ability to
actually use protein to build and
maintain muscle tissue, becomes less
efficient. You need more protein than
you did at 50, not less, and you need it
spread across meals, not concentrated in
one sitting.
The current evidence supports a protein
target of 1.0 to 1.2 g per kilogram of
body weight per day for adults over 70
who are moderately active.
For a 150-lb adult, that's approximately
68 to 82 g per day. For a 130-lb adult,
roughly 59 to 71 g. A study published in
the American Journal of Clinical
Nutrition found that older adults who
distributed protein evenly across three
meals, rather than concentrating it at
dinner, showed significantly greater
rates of muscle protein synthesis over a
24-hour period. The body can only
effectively use approximately 25 to 40 g
of protein per meal for muscle
synthesis.
Eating 60 g at dinner does not give you
double the benefit. Much of it is simply
processed and eliminated. Practical
guidance, aim for 20 to 30 g of protein
at each meal. Breakfast options include
eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, or a
simple protein shake. Lunch might be
fish, chicken, legumes, or tofu. Dinner
follows naturally. Leucine-rich protein
sources, eggs, fish, dairy, poultry, are
particularly effective at stimulating
muscle protein synthesis in older
adults. The common mistake is treating
protein as something primarily for
athletes or bodybuilders. In reality,
adequate protein after 70 is one of the
most protective things you can do for
your independence. Every day without
enough protein is a day your body is
borrowing from your muscle reserves.
Habit five, this is the one that
surprises people most, not because it's
complicated, but because they never
imagined it belonged in a conversation
about physical health. Meaningful social
engagement, every single day, not
weekly, not when it's convenient, every
day. And I want to explain exactly why,
because the research here is not subtle.
Thomas was 81. He lived alone. He had
phone calls with his kids a few times a

content. He wasn't suffering. He wasn't
depressed, not in any way he recognized.
